cards.front: To whom must drivers yield crosswalk right-of-way under the Iowa law from twenty twenty-four?
cards.back: A twenty twenty-four Iowa law orders drivers to yield crosswalk right-of-way to people on foot and to riders of any human-powered device, called a pedestrian conveyance.

cards.front: What counts as a pedestrian conveyance?
cards.back: A conveyance is any human-powered device used to get around without walking or to move another person, including wheelchairs, strollers, skateboards, scooters, and electric personal assistive mobility devices.

cards.front: Whom does the word pedestrian cover throughout the manual?
cards.back: Every use of the word pedestrian in the manual covers both walkers and conveyance riders.

cards.front: How do crosswalk rights compare between walkers and conveyance riders?
cards.back: Walkers and conveyance riders share identical crosswalk rights, since the manual folds every human-powered device into its pedestrian term.

cards.front: How does the manual class skateboards and scooters?
cards.back: Skateboards and scooters count as pedestrian conveyances with full crosswalk rights, not as vehicles.

cards.front: What does a reflective orange triangle on a vehicle's rear mean?
cards.back: A reflective orange triangle on a vehicle's rear means it travels at thirty-five miles per hour or less, as seen on maintenance rigs, farm vehicles, and horse-drawn wagons.

cards.front: What do mile markers count, and what are they used for?
cards.back: Guide signs give directions and distances to cities, airports, borders, parks, and museums, while mile markers count miles from the state line for exit math and emergency location.

cards.front: What do service signs point to?
cards.back: Service signs point to rest areas, fuel, campgrounds, and hospitals.

cards.front: How do guide, service, and route signs divide their jobs?
cards.back: Guide signs name places and distances, service signs name traveler comforts, and route signs name the road itself by shape.
cards.memory_hook: Guide places, service comforts, route road

cards.front: Whose traffic directions must you follow?
cards.back: Officers, highway workers, and school crossing guards may direct traffic, and you must follow their directions.

cards.front: How do solid red and flashing red signals differ?
cards.back: Solid red orders a complete stop, while flashing red is handled exactly like a stop sign.
cards.memory_hook: Solid red stop, flashing stop sign

cards.front: What should you do on a solid yellow light?
cards.back: On solid yellow, hold back when you can stop safely and otherwise clear the intersection with care.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow signal mean?
cards.back: Flashing yellow means advance with caution, yielding to vehicles and pedestrians until the way is safe.

cards.front: What does a solid green signal allow?
cards.back: Solid green means go only when the way is clear, yielding to anyone still inside and letting trapped traffic clear after the change.

cards.front: What separates solid red from flashing red in what they order?
cards.back: Solid red orders a full stop for through traffic, while flashing red turns the signal into a stop sign for every approach.

cards.front: How does solid yellow differ from flashing yellow?
cards.back: Solid yellow asks whether you can stop, demanding a hold when possible, while flashing yellow grants passage conditioned only on caution and yielding.

cards.front: What does a steady red arrow require of turning drivers?
cards.back: A steady red arrow forces turning drivers to stop.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow arrow warn?
cards.back: A steady yellow arrow warns the turn signal is going red, so hold back when stoppable and finish the turn only from inside the intersection.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow arrow let you do?
cards.back: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, since the opposing lanes hold green.

cards.front: What does a steady green arrow permit and forbid?
cards.back: A steady green arrow permits the indicated turn while oncoming traffic waits, yet forbids going straight and still requires giving way to anyone already inside.

cards.front: How do the steady red arrow and the flashing yellow arrow differ?
cards.back: The steady red arrow forbids the turn outright, while the flashing yellow arrow permits a left after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

cards.front: What is the difference between the steady yellow arrow and the steady green arrow?
cards.back: The steady yellow arrow warns a protected turn is ending, while the steady green arrow grants the turn but never the straight path.

cards.front: Why must you never halt on railroad tracks?
cards.back: Treat every rail crossing with extra care and never halt on the tracks, since trains cannot brake fast and advance signs plus pavement markings announce the rails ahead.

cards.front: What should you do near the tracks to sense a train?
cards.back: Near the tracks, drop distractions, roll the windows down, and silence the music so you can sense a train.

cards.front: What does each crossing post for reporting problems?
cards.back: Each crossing posts its railroad name with an emergency number to call for signal faults, stalls, obstructions, or track damage.

cards.front: What do flashing lights or lowered gates at a crossing mean?
cards.back: At gated or lighted crossings, flashing lights or lowered gates mean a train is coming, so obey them and never cross or weave around a gate.

cards.front: What marks a passive crossing, and what should you do there?
cards.back: Passive crossings show only a crossbuck with a stop or yield sign, so slow down, look for the train, and always expect one.

cards.front: How do active and passive crossings differ?
cards.back: Active crossings command obedience to lights and gates, while passive crossings offer only a crossbuck with a stop or yield sign and demand a visual check.

cards.front: Where may you cross tracks, and what should you remember about ungated tracks?
cards.back: Cross tracks only at marked crossings, heed every sign and signal, and remember that ungated tracks still carry trains announced by advance signs and markings.

cards.front: Why do rail cars wear reflective stripes?
cards.back: Rail cars wear reflective stripes for night and murky weather, so scan for the train itself before rolling across.

cards.front: What should you assume about trains at any crossing?
cards.back: Always expect a train, which may run closer and faster than it looks on any track at any time, with extra tracks meaning extra trains, so confirm a clear view both ways first and never try to beat one.

cards.front: When waiting at a crossing, how far must you keep from the closest rail, and what must you never do mid-crossing?
cards.back: Cross only when sure of clearing fully, since trains overhang the rails; when waiting, keep fifteen feet between your vehicle and the closest rail, and never shift gears mid-crossing.

cards.front: What is the difference between the fifteen-foot waiting gap and the fifteen-to-fifty-foot band?
cards.back: The fifteen-foot waiting gap keeps a stopped car clear of the nearest rail, while the fifteen-to-fifty band marks where buses and hazmat must halt before crossing.

cards.front: Who is credited for the illustrated guide to rail signs and signals that follows the crossing rules?
cards.back: The page after the rail-crossing rules holds an illustrated guide to rail signs and signals credited to Operation Lifesaver.

cards.front: Which vehicles must halt fifteen to fifty feet before the rails, and what excuses the stop?
cards.back: School and charter buses, hired-ride drivers, and placarded hazmat haulers must halt fifteen to fifty feet before the rails, then cross; an officer's or signal's order to proceed and a posted EXEMPT sign both excuse the stop.

cards.front: How does the crossing rule for buses and hazmat haulers differ from the rule for other drivers?
cards.back: Buses, hired rides, and hazmat haulers must always halt short of the rails, while other drivers halt for flashing lights and lowered gates.

cards.front: If you stall on the tracks with a train near, how should you leave the vehicle?
cards.back: Stalled on the tracks with a train near, keep cranking the starter until the train shows, stand clear waving at the engineer, then get everyone out at once and walk clear of the rails at a forty-five-degree angle toward the oncoming train.

cards.front: If you are stuck at a crossing with no train in sight, what should you do?
cards.back: Stuck or stalled at a crossing, empty the vehicle and run far even with no train in sight, then phone the blue-and-white ENS sign's number with its crossing ID, or call emergency services at nine-one-one when no sign stands.
cards.memory_hook: Empty, run, call ENS or nine-one-one

cards.front: How does a stall with a train in view differ from one with no train in view?
cards.back: A stall with a train in view adds restart attempts and engineer-waving to the evacuation, while a stall with no train in view goes straight to evacuation plus the ENS call.
cards.memory_hook: Train seen: restart, wave; none: call

cards.front: What devices and signs do work zones add?
cards.back: Work zones add arrow boards, temporary signals, flaggers, and channelizing hardware, with mostly diamond-shaped orange signs and only a few rectangles.

cards.front: What do work-zone devices mark, and why stay sharp?
cards.back: Those devices mark construction, maintenance, survey, and utility work, steering drivers and walkers past the crew; stay sharp because fines may double there.

cards.front: How should you drive through a work zone?
cards.back: In work zones, match speed to conditions, obey every sign, signal, and flagger, stretch your following gap, and lock your full attention on driving.

cards.front: What do big flashing arrow panels usually signal?
cards.back: Big flashing arrow panels usually signal a closed lane or shoulder.

cards.front: How do flaggers direct work traffic, and what do they wear?
cards.back: Flaggers with stop-or-slow paddles direct work traffic and must be obeyed; they wear fluorescent yellow-green or orange and mostly use paddle signs, with red flags only at times.

cards.front: What do barricades, upright panels, drums, cones, and tube markers do?
cards.back: Barricades, upright panels, drums, cones, and tube markers warn of odd or risky layouts and funnel drivers safely through.

cards.front: How do arrow boards, channelizing hardware, and flaggers share the work-zone job?
cards.back: Arrow boards announce closures, channelizing hardware steers the path, and flaggers direct traffic with paddles that must be obeyed.
